This study provides a detailed examination of the potential inaccuracies in
the output of contextualized language models when analyzing diachronic semantic
shifts in word meanings. We present an enhanced ensemble method that surpasses
earlier contextualized approaches and apply it to investigate the levels of
semantic change in English vocabulary over a 20-year span, using the
Corpus
Common
Search (C2) corpus. Our analysis reveals that contextualized methods may
mislead researchers into concluding there have been significant semantic
transformations in words that have actually remained constant. We further
demonstrate how non-linguistic factors, such as word frequency and genre
composition, can contribute to the apparent instances of semantic change.

Active galactic nuclei (AGNs), containing accreting black holes at their center, allow for the investigation of black hole mass and spin through the analysis of electromagnetic spectra. This research uses the Spin-Modified Fundamental Plane of black hole activity, a non-linear model that links radio luminosity, optical or X-ray luminosity, black hole mass, and spin. Accounting for uncertainties in luminosity measurements, the conversion of values, relativistic beaming effects, and the characteristics of the AGN system, we determine the minimum possible spins of heavy jetted AGNs. These results help explore the relationship between the masses of ultra-light scalar, vector, and tensor particles, closing a gap in parameter space around $10^{-20}-10^{-19}$eV. Additionally, we determine the upper limits on the decay constant of axions, assuming their decay could prevent their entry into a state of instability and their possible non-observation through superradiance. This research also provides upper limits on the fraction of dark matter comprised by ultra-light axion-like particles, concluding that, as a single species, such a particle cannot constitute more than 10% of the dark matter in a given mass range ($10^{-21} < \mu \, (\mathrm{eV}) < 10^{-17}$).

A distinctive feature of neural development is the rhythmic shifting of cell nuclei
between the upper and lower layers of the neuroepithelial tissue as interkinetic nuclear
migration (IKNM) unfolds. In this study, we utilize extended, high-speed lightsheet and two-photon imaging
techniques in live zebrafish retinas during initial development to gain insights into the underlying mechanisms governing
the behavior of cell nuclei during IKNM. Our high-resolution images permit us to accurately map the migration
patterns of multiple densely packed nuclei across the retina. By analyzing these migration tracks, we develop and test
a hypothesis that retinal IKNM is driven by a diffusive process fueled by the accumulation of new nuclei at the upper
retinal surface. Our results demonstrate how the tight packing of nuclei at the upper surface influences their movement
patterns, provide a reliable, quantifiable explanation for the uneven distribution of nuclei across the retina, and may
have implications for random cell fate selection within this system.

In various image processing tasks, including video compressed sensing and color image demosaicing, images must be separated from coded measurements that represent their superposition. Real-world code patterns, which are often non-negative, systematically structured and non-Gaussian, can impede reconstruction performance due to their non-ideal coherence properties. This research addresses this challenge by developing optimized code patterns that minimize the coherence of the sensing matrix and signal representation matrix combination, taking into consideration their inherent structural properties, specifically non-negativity, block-diagonal structure, and circular shifting, which are particularly beneficial for certain compressed sensing architectures, facilitating accurate and seamless reconstruction of compressed images.

We've developed a comprehensive hydrodynamic theory that applies to polar active fluids in the presence of randomly distributed inclusions, and our model demonstrates the possibility of overcoming these obstructions to maintain a non-zero overall speed. Contrary to previous assumptions, the dynamics of this specific class of active matter cannot be accurately described using simplified hydrodynamic models when the spatial environment is two-dimensional or three-dimensional for large-scale spatial variations. Moreover, the distinct small-scale dynamics exhibit different statistical characteristics in 2D and 3D space, demonstrating the importance of considering detailed spatial interactions in understanding the fundamental dynamics of these systems.

The growth of Information Technology has significantly altered how information is shared, making it necessary to convert printed documents into digital formats.  There has been an increase in fraudulent activities lately.  To prevent such account-related fraud, a system was devised which employs ID card extraction via OCR and NLP for verification purposes.  Optical Character Recognition, a technology that enables the conversion of images to text, can also be used to convert an Indonesian ID card or KTP into text format.  This facilitates easier data entry for service operators.  To enhance accuracy, the extracted text was further corrected using Natural Language Processing.  When tested using 50 Indonesian ID card images, the F-score achieved was 0.78, and the extraction process for each ID card took approximately 4510 milliseconds.

Quantum harmonic oscillators were computationally analyzed in their ground state with either steady-state driving forces varying in intensity or driving forces that changed over time. Calculations of position expectations were carried out for multiple scenarios of mass, angular frequency, and both classical and quantum widths in the latter case. For steady-state conditions, orientation phases of the wave packet were tested with different scenarios. The simulation approach was validated by comparing results to established theoretical outcomes.

The Yarkovsky-O'Keefe-Radzievskii-Paddack effect significantly impacts the rotational states of small asteroids by exerting a net torque resulting from solar radiation reflected and re-emitted by the surface. As a consequence of this phenomenon, the rotation period of these asteroids gradually changes, which can be best measured through light curves as the phase shift accumulates over time in a quadratic manner. To study this effect in detail, researchers collected archived data and conducted new photometric observations for asteroids 1992 SK, Geographos, and Toro, before utilizing a light curve inversion method to match their shapes and rotation characteristics. By modeling the YORP effect and incorporating other relevant parameters into their analysis, scientists were able to detect the YORP acceleration in three asteroids and found that the YORP acceleration in all ten detected cases was positive, accelerating their rotations. Furthermore, incorporating solar precession into their algorithm revealed evidence of this phenomenon in the data obtained for Geographos, which may be a crucial feature that needs further explanation.

We show that any subgroup of homeomorphisms of a compact surface that fix the boundary, whose action within the surface's interior is highly transitive, cannot be topologically compact when using the compact-open topology's inherited structure.

Multiple formal models can equivalently define functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings, including MSO-transducers, streaming transducers, and certain two-way transducers. However, even when restricted to single passes through the input, some functions in these models can still be undecidable by Turing machines with infinite input, despite being defined by finite-state machines. To address this issue, a new decision-making approach is proposed for determining whether a specific function is computable and if so, to create a corresponding Turing machine. 

For the specific case of computable functions that map infinite strings to other infinite strings and satisfy a specific decidability property, this approach involves characterizing and identifying a sub-class of realizable functions within the streaming transducer model. The intended class of functions is also described using an alternative model, known as the MSO-transducer. Notably, a key result is established which connects the decision-making approach to another property called rational continuity and if so, to convert this format into the streaming transducer model.

A machine learning technique known as reservoir computing generates a model that mimics complex systems and can be trained on significantly smaller amounts of data compared to alternative methods. The latest version of this approach simplifies training by minimizing the need to adjust numerous parameters. In a recent experiment involving a highly complex system with distinct time scales and multiple coexisting patterns of behavior, a reservoir computer of the new design demonstrated several advantages over its traditional counterpart. Specifically, it used a much smaller amount of data for training, a much shorter time to pattern recognition, and a smaller number of parameters for an accurate prediction model. Furthermore, it was found that the new design performed better in pattern recognition when pattern stability varied widely, but this performance could be enhanced by incorporating a more tailored time scale transformation.

To address scalability issues with Eulerian methods for finding optimal controllers under constraints and worst-case disturbances in variational Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs formulations, we've developed a second-order successive sweep algorithm for calculating the reachable state space. This approach, which assumes a continuous and smooth Hamilton-Jacobi-Isaacs equation, enables us to determine the states that can be reached within a given time frame under worst-case conditions and state feedback control.

The underlying mechanisms of the ventral temporal cortex's animacy organization remain contentious, suggesting that animacy exists along a spectrum rather than a binary divide. Recent evidence suggests this continuum is influenced by the degree of presence or absence of distinct animal features or by how entities are perceived as social agents. In this study, a stimulus set with independent factors of visual categorizability and agency perception in animals was used to test these hypotheses through both computational neural networks and behavioral experiments. Utilizing functional magnetic resonance imaging, our findings showed that visual categorizability and agency perception separately explained independent components of the animacy spectrum in VTC. When combined, they fully captured the continuum, and our data indicated distinct posterior regions associated with each. The results of this study demonstrate the complex nature of the animacy spectrum in VTC, revealing multiple governing principles such as social agency that shape our understanding of this phenomenon.

The study proves the nonexistence of Landau-Siegel zeros or confirms quantum unique ergodicity for GL_2 Hecke-Maass newforms at a calculable pace. Additionally, it establishes the same result for GL_N Hecke-Maass newforms (where N is fixed) for a broader set of measures, specifically confirming the absence of exceptional zeros or demonstrating the distribution of mass of Eisenstein series in the limit, both of which can be applied to prove the duality between GL_N and PGL_2.

We have adapted the quantum relational Hoare logic originally proposed in (Unruh, POPL 2019) to incorporate "expectations" into preconditions and postconditions, thereby enabling the quantification of pre-/postconditions that reflect the relationship between programs' inputs and outputs when comparing pairs of programs.

The rapid transmission of contagious diseases is frequently intensified by a single high-transmission event, a super-spreader occurrence. This effect should be given considerable attention in formulating infection transmission models and subsequently in designing effective public health interventions. A key feature of a super-spreader event is its ability to circumvent typical constraints on transmission rates imposed by the population's physical density. To model this effect, we developed a two-population susceptible-infected model, incorporating a delay between the two populations during super-spreader events, and we analyzed it in contrast to standard mixing scenarios. Our model shows that standard epidemiological interventions, such as social distancing and mask-wearing, may significantly influence the course of an outbreak but are limited in their capacity to fully prevent a super-spreader event. The risk of extinction of a disease is reduced as temperatures rise, regardless of transmissibility, and it increases with transmission rates derived from such events.

Let's consider a complex topological vector space, denoted as X, along with the collection L(X) of continuous linear operators that act on X. This paper seeks to expand the concept of codiskcyclicity, initially developed for a solitary operator within L(X), to a broader context of operator sets defined as $\Gamma\subset L(X).$ Some key results regarding codiskcyclic collections of operators are proven, accompanied by a codiskcyclicity criterion. Furthermore, we demonstrate its practical utility by investigating the codiskcyclicity of C_0-semigroups comprised of operators.

The paper addresses the problem of bias in vector magnetic field maps, particularly in estimating the component perpendicular to the line-of-sight, Bperp. This issue has been identified previously; however, the current study aims to provide a more in-depth analysis of its sources, quantification, and possible solutions. Initially, the authors establish precise metrics to assess Bperp bias, accounting for both local and native components. Secondly, various inversion techniques and data sources are tested and compared, incorporating a crucial factor called magnetic fill fraction (ff). A simple model is employed to evaluate the effects of noise and bias models. The results reveal that the bias primarily affects high-contrast magnetic features, noise exacerbates this problem, and the bias models' performance is comparable to the previously successful "reprojection" method. Importantly, the models' success is attributed to the inclusion of ff as input. Additionally, the studies had the notable benefit of identifying successives steps to test future bias-reduction algorithms.

A sign problem encountered in Monte Carlo simulations beyond half-filling can be mitigated by transforming the integration path. However, this transformation introduces an additional computational cost associated with the Jacobian determinant in the Boltzmann weight, posing a significant barrier for large-scale simulations. Our proposed architecture, based on a novel application of complex-valued affine coupling layers in neural networks, efficiently circumvents this challenge by achieving linear scaling of the determinant cost. As a result, this method allows us to tackle intractably large systems plagued by a severe sign problem.

Given any non-erasing free monoid morphism σ and subshift X, its image subshift Y under σ and the associated complexity functions p_X and p_Y exhibit the following relationship: there exist constants c, d, and C, where p_X scales by a factor of at least c times d, while scaling at most C, in the sufficiently large integers n in N. If σ is recognizable and letter-to-letter, then p_Y and p_X grow at similar rates, whereas if σ isn't letter-to-letter, there are instances where p_X isn't proportional to p_Y. As a result, topological entropy h_X isn't necessarily preserved when applying σ, indicating that defining topological entropy for free group currents F_N isn't feasible. Nevertheless, we can distinguish currents with or without zero or positive topological entropy.

By leveraging previously acquired skills and adapting them to unfamiliar tasks without explicit guidance, humans demonstrate impressive cross-task capabilities.
This study aims to enhance the cross-task generalization ability of massive language models in unsupervised settings, with a focus on models like T0 and FLAN.
We introduce a novel, unsupervised retrieval-augmentation method known as ReCross, which employs unlabeled samples to selectively draw from existing data, fine-tune the model for better performance.
The proposed method seamlessly integrates both high-efficiency dense retrieval and a more effective pair-wise re-ranking process to produce outstanding results, surpassing non-retrieval methods and alternative baselines in our experiments.

Optimizing hyperparameters in the private version of the stochastic gradient descent algorithm is a critical issue due to limited access to private datasets for hyperparameter tuning. The development of algorithms that efficiently find optimal hyperparameters for a favorable balance between privacy and performance within a predetermined search space is, therefore, crucial. In this paper, a generalized framework is established to determine an optimal balance between privacy and performance, and three cost-effective algorithms are systematically examined within this framework: evolutionary optimization, Bayesian methods, and reinforcement learning. The results of our experiments, conducted using MNIST and CIFAR-10 datasets for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning, show significant improvements over the conventional grid search method. The paper addresses existing challenges and potential research directions in the field, and provides an open-source code for hyperparameter tuning in private deep learning.

For a Coxeter system denoted by (W,S), we develop the concept of a boolean complex consisting of involutions within W, mirroring Ragnarsson and Tenner's previous work. By applying discrete Morse theory, we identify the homotopy type of this boolean complex for a significant subset of Coxeter groups, including finite groups, revealing that its homotopy type is equivalent to that of a collection of spheres with dimension |S|-1. Moreover, we derive straightforward, recursive formulas to compute the number of spheres within this collection.

We applied an advanced statistical approach to examine the composition of 34,410 stars in the Milky Way disk using a vast dataset from the APOGEE-2. The study involved using a two-component model to break down elemental patterns into supernovae types and then comparing observed values to predicted values. The comparison yielded small discrepancies of up to 0.1 dex in some cases. The research revealed relationships between elements including a group sharing similar variations and distinct groups of elements with different behaviors. It also shed light on stars that the model struggled to accurately account for, often finding they were related in space and time, though the origin of some exceptions remains unclear. The study identified potential barriers to mixing elements in the disk and offered insights into which galaxies would be most beneficial to observe with similar spectroscopic techniques. The research results are expected to be useful for identifying planets around stars and as standard references for other chemical analyses. The dataset and code are available for public use.

The COVID-19 pandemic spread globally in early 2020, causing severe health and economic consequences in China specifically. In this context, research is crucial to understand how rumors propagate online and measure their impact effectively. Researchers have analyzed 10 prevalent rumors along with COVID-19 in Chinese social media, incorporating comments from prominent media outlets and expert opinions. A striking finding revealed that misinformation tends to decline exponentially over time, diverging significantly from the pattern of factual information. Furthermore, an individual's influence in shaping the discourse was discovered to be dynamically linked to their content's propagation range, rather than being fixed. This unique connection remains consistent across various languages, cultures, and time periods. To capture this intricate relationship, a new metric called the Upward Spread Force (USF) is proposed to assess an individual's influence dynamically. The study's results provide actionable insights for identifying, monitoring, and countering misinformation effectively within communities, organizations, and governments.

A novel approach to measuring the distance to galaxies has been discovered by examining extragalactic planetary nebulae, specifically due to their nearly universal brightness pattern. Determining the precise distances to galaxies through planetary nebulae analysis depends on collecting comprehensive data sets, and the observed frequency of these nebulae directly correlates with the galaxies' overall mass. Therefore, researchers must either utilize wide-field observations or focus on the central areas of galaxies. By focusing on the central areas, a comprehensive study has been conducted of the planetary nebulae residing within early-type galaxies located within the Fornax cluster using spectroscopic observations taken from the VLT/MUSE data collection from the Fornax3D survey. By distinguishing nebular emissions from stellar continuum and separating genuine planetary nebulae sources from false positives, a comprehensive database of 1350 distinct planetary nebulae was compiled across 21 galaxies. Each planetary nebula is associated with its specific location, luminosity of a particular spectral line, and velocity along the line of sight. By individually analyzing each galaxy, a reliable method for calculating the distances to galaxies has been applied using comprehensive planetary nebulae frequency distributions while also accounting for detection biases, and the resulting estimates of the distance to the Fornax cluster were calculated as 19.86 megaparsecs with an associated margin of error. Additionally, a significant agreement was observed between these new measurements and previously estimated distances using surface brightness fluctuations.

Every day, hospitals around the world gather vast amounts of physiological data from their patients, leading to an escalating interest in conducting statistical analyses to provide better medical diagnoses. These analyses involve complex computations on significant datasets, necessitating high-performance data processing systems that can balance efficiency and simplicity. To address the limitations of existing data processing solutions, we present \emph{LifeStream}, a robust stream processing engine specifically designed to handle physiological data efficiently. LifeStream optimizes performance while providing intuitive temporal query language support, thus striking a balance between ease of programming and computational speed. Furthermore, LifeStream exhibits superior performance, outperforming other leading stream processing engines and hand-tuned numerical libraries by up to $7.5\times$ and $3.2\times$ respectively, on realistic datasets and workload simulations.

This research paper confirms that certain types of curves, specifically those in higher dimensional space, do not fit the classification of Bertrand curves except in two-dimensional Euclidean space. A new category, called the timelike (1,3)-Bertrand curve, is defined to fill this gap and its characteristics are identified for curves in a four-dimensional Euclidean space.

The choice of loss function for a neural network is widely regarded as a key decision with far-reaching implications, given the numerous loss functions developed to date, making it crucial to carefully select one. Despite its significance, research on the topic often omits explicit justification for loss function selection. We contend that this lack of justification reflects an untested assumption prevalent within the deep learning community. In this research, we investigate how loss function impacts performance in a supervised classification context. Our findings reveal that certain, previously underappreciated loss functions, including the KL divergence, can yield superior outcomes compared to established methods, underscoring the need to view loss function choice as a parameter amenable to optimization, rather than a fixed constant.

This research aims to advance the understanding of thermomechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region formation, degradation, and temperature changes during cyclic loading tests. Numerical implementation based on the finite element method provides the basis for numerical solutions, which include simulations of material sample microstructure and temperature evolution.

To analyze the impact of external magnetization on doped Bi$_2$Se$_3$ with spin-triplet nematic superconductivity, we computationally investigate magnetic susceptibility in nematic and chiral superconducting states using the Ginzburg-Landau formalism near its critical temperature. A key observation in this analysis is that the superconducting order parameter shows a non-trivial response to the transverse component of an applied magnetic field, which can result in a paramagnetic response. Moreover, the topology of the Fermi surface exerts a substantial influence on magnetic susceptibility, with a specific Lifshitz transition inducing a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase and leading to the divergence of magnetic susceptibility at this transition point. Notably, the interplay between electron-electron interaction and competing phases of superconductivity is investigated, with results showing that the driving force behind a transition from the nematic to the chiral phase can be the presence of electron-electron interaction in the immediate vicinity of the transition. A comparison with existing experimental data is also presented in this analysis.

Continuous phase modulation detection using conventional differential detection techniques is highly resistant to various channel disturbances, such as phase and Doppler shift. Its basic structure makes its implementation uncomplicated, involving the product of a received baseband signal and a time-reversed version of one symbol duration. Nevertheless, it experiences reduced signal-to-noise ratio compared to coherent detection methods. In this research, the performance of conventional differential detection is enhanced through increased delay periods. By accounting for $K$ symbol delays, the trellis structure and relevant branch and cumulative metrics are derived, resulting in an optimized criterion for $K$. This criterion is based on the minimum Euclidean distance between differential signals, ultimately facilitating the selection of ideal delay periods for popular CPM formats through simulated error rates verification.

A previously reported finding from the research of the 1990s and 2000s is the strikingly uniform value of the ratio of variations to the mean in the energy density of quantum fields across various spacetime settings. Initially calculated using correlators of quantum field stress-energy tensors, the issue will now be re-examined using quantum thermodynamics. This is accomplished by determining the thermodynamic quantities known as heat capacity and quantum compressibility in model spacetimes filled with a quantum field at both high and low temperatures. The proportion of these fluctuations to the mean value of the energy density is determined. Determining the ratio of variance to the mean value of the Stokes parameter provides an assessment of our confidence in using a classical statistical distribution to describe the local distribution of energy densities. The results are valid for various quantum field states, including those that are flat, squeezed, or squeezed with symmetry in Minkowski space. The findings are also applicable to the Bunch-Davies state in de Sitter space. The calculations carried out are expected to support the validity of general quantum field theory correlators.

Our proposed dataset, ATOMIC, is an exhaustive collection of everyday commonsense reasoning rules comprising nearly a million text-based descriptions.  This atlas of inferential knowledge, structured as conditional relationships (if X, then Y), stands out from other available datasets that are centered on categorization, by providing a framework that accounts for causality and effects, actions versus thoughts, and intentional versus unintentional actions.  We have developed nine categories of these relationships and demonstrated the efficacy of incorporating these patterns into models of artificial intelligence.  Our findings reveal that through generative training on ATOMIC, our models have gained a capacity for basic reasoning about events that are novel.  This is supported by test results showing that machine learning models incorporating these patterns achieve more accurate outcomes in relation to models operating in isolation as judged by both automated assessments and human feedback.

Portfolio optimization is a critical application in Finance, yet its computational intricacies compel financial institutions to resort to simplified methods that require considerable time. By leveraging the Lagrange multiplier method, the mean-variance portfolio optimization issue can be formulated into a collection of simplified linear equations, facilitating efficient resolution via the HHL algorithm. Nevertheless, the HHL algorithm's reliance on sparse Hamiltonians and hybrid-classical-quantum functionality presents significant hurdles for implementation on Noisy Intermediate Scale Quantum devices. To tackle these challenges, this paper introduces NISQ-HHL: a revised HHL algorithm suited for near-term hardware, and utilizes NISQ-HHL to compute optimal portfolios across various portfolios, pricing models, and noise models, employing both the HHL and classical methods for comparative analysis. The results indicate that NISQ-HHL yields precise outcomes comparable to the classical algorithm, but also highlights the necessity of developing a streamlined exponential decay sampler to ensure the feasibility of HHL on NISQ devices. Consequently, this paperH's findings Hoffer Hprovide Hvalue Hfor Hplanning Hwith HNISQ hardware.

To enhance data efficiency of state-of-the-art end-to-end ASR models and enable them to handle a large amount of unpaired text data through multi-modal training, it's essential to address two challenges: synchronizing the sampling rates of speech and language features and ensuring that the learned representations from both encoders are consistent. This paper introduces a novel bidirectional attention mechanism that combines the learning of both the ASR and text encoders using a multi-modal learning method. This attention mechanism facilitates the exchange of sampling rates, effectively allowing the model to learn from sentences consisting of individual characters. This leads to a robust, unified representation that effectively incorporates the features extracted by both the ASR and text encoders. As demonstrated in experiments, this approach yields a significant 6.3% reduction in word error rate on the Librispeech test set when trained with only 10% of the paired data, and achieves an 11.3% improvement when utilizing unpaired text data.

This paper investigates the long-term behavior of a randomly generated uniform parking distribution of size $n$, denoted as $\pi_n$. We establish that the first $k_n$ positions of $\pi_n$, $\pi_n(1)$ through $\pi_n(k_n)$, are asymptotically independent and identically distributed with a uniform probability distribution over the set $\{1, 2, \dots, n\}$ for two different distance metrics. When the number of initial positions $k_n$ grows at a rate slower than $\sqrt{n}$ for the total variation distance and slower than $n$ for the Kolmogorov distance, this asymptotic behavior is shown, thereby extending previous findings by Diaconis and Hicks. Furthermore, this work also derives rate bounds and statistical limit theorems for the sum or the maximum of the first $k_n$ parking locations. Our main approach to achieving these results is by utilizing conditioned random walk reformulations.

Measurements of superconducting nanowires, particularly NbN nanowires, indicate the presence of a critical voltage threshold for dc conduction below which coherent quantum phase slips dominate, potentially blocking conduction. The critical voltage of these nanowires is observed to be tunable using an adjacent gate electrode and varies significantly in response to applied voltage, aligning with expected results of quantum interference but exhibiting unanticipated periodic variations. The magnitude of these periodic variations far exceeds predictions based on capacitance alone and presents a discrepancy in understanding this phenomenon, especially after observing sudden period shifts during measurements. The possibility of attributing the behavior to granular Josephson junctions within the nanowires is also considered, offering an alternative explanation for the findings.

Our proposed approach tackles the challenge of novel view video prediction, taking input from multiple viewpoints. Unlike existing research that relies on narrow angle variations, our network can generate videos from significantly wider angles, up to 45 degrees, without the need for prior knowledge. By processing only RGB frames, we've developed a two-component representation, combining local and global features that enables novel view prediction. Our model achieves remarkable results on real-world datasets NTU-RGB+D and CMU Panoptic, surpassing the state-of-the-art in novel view video prediction, demonstrating significant gains in SSIM, PSNR, and FVD scores of 26.1%, 13.6%, and 60% respectively, without the use of prior views.

In this research, inter-orbital coupling was demonstrated using femtosecond laser writing, which enables orthogonal modes in a photonic lattice to couple with each other at different spatial locations. We characterized an asymmetric double-well structure, mapped its propagation dynamics and successfully created a device capable of spatial mode conversion anywhere within a photonic chip. Utilizing higher-order photonic mode phase structure, our experiment showed that a trimer configuration can serve as a $\pi$-phase beam splitter for multiplexing and other interference-based photonic applications.

The Ω-baryon, which contains sss quarks and has only been marginally detected in past experiments, has primarily been studied using theoretical methods so far. A study aims to explore this particle's properties utilizing a quark model with linear confining forces. Calculated resonance masses are presented for the ground and excited states of S, P, D, and F quark systems. A linear nature of the Regge trajectory, supported by calculated data and magnetic moments, has also been examined. This study compares its results to other approaches and available experimental evidence.

Airborne transmission risk in confined environments like buses is intricately affected by the interplay between turbulent airflow, respiration processes, coughing, and sneezing, as well as various ventilation methods, temperature-driven buoyancy effects, and surface deposition of aerosols. To better understand and quantify this complex dynamic, we used numerical models of unsteady airflow to analyze and visualize virus-laden aerosol transport. In comparing our detailed model to a widely accepted 'well mixed' model, notable discrepancies in the distribution of aerosol particles became evident, with implications for our understanding of the spread of airborne pathogens. Furthermore, the differences identified in our study are expected to be relevant to a broader range of enclosed settings beyond urban buses.

The Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect involves a rise in Spin-Orbit Coupling near a strong spin-orbit material's interface with an adjacent layer. This phenomenon has been observed in various systems, such as graphene and ferromagnetic layers, and controlling Spin-Orbit Coupling may lead to the discovery of novel phases in superconductor and semimetallic systems. In the study presented here, magnetoelectrical transport, specifically magnetoresistance and the anomalous Hall effect, were investigated in Cobalt/Bismuth multilayers in search of Spin-Orbit Proximity Effect and an analysis of its origin. Findings suggest that very thin Cobalt layers exhibit increased Spontaneous Magnetic Anisotropy of Resistivity and Anomalous Hall Resistivity. An examination of Anomalous Hall Resisitivity revealed that the Bismuth layers modify the Hall effect's scattering mechanism to the extrinsic skew-scattering type, suggesting that the spin-orbit proximity effect could result from elastic scattering of Cobalt's free carriers by Bismuth sites at the interface.

This paper provides approximate solutions to the fractional time-independent Schrödinger equation in $N$-dimensional space for a generalised Mie-type potential, expressed as $V(r^{\alpha})=A/r^{2\alpha} + B/r^{\alpha} + C$, with the fractional parameter $\alpha$ affecting the space variable $r$. As $\alpha$ equals 1, the potential becomes the original Mie-type potential, commonly studied in physics. Using the Jumarie type fractional derivative approach, solutions are obtained and expressed in terms of the Mittag-Leffler function and a fractionally defined confluent hypergeometric function. Verification of results is achieved by comparison with existing works, particularly for $\alpha=1$. Numerical examples, including a diatomic molecule, demonstrate energy eigenvalue and bound state eigenfunction calculations.

We analyze how enforcing a neural network's Lipschitz continuity, as it pertains to input sensitivity, affects its performance. In order to investigate this, we developed a straightforward approach to determine the upper bound for a neural network's Lipschitz constant, taking into consideration various $p$-norms commonly used. This approach enables us to frame training a neural network with a limited Lipschitz constant as an optimisation problem that can be resolved via constrained stochastic gradient descent. Through our experiments, we found that models trained using this approach consistently performed better than those using alternative methods of regularisation. We further found that selecting hyperparameters is relatively straightforward and demonstrated the relationship between chosen norms and the resulting model's performance. The benefits of our approach are especially apparent when neural networks are trained on limited datasets.

We investigate the possibility of lepton-flavour non-universality in certain processes at the Large Hadron Collider (LHC). To this end, we focus on Drell-Yan ditau production and calculate precise corrections to this process, taking into account the effects of quantum chromodynamics at the next-to-leading order. A specialized code is developed to efficiently generate these corrections, allowing for more accurate simulations of ditau events. By applying these simulations to recent LHC data, we can place constraints on a type of exotic particle, known as vector leptoquarks, based on their mass and coupling strength. This code is an important tool for ongoing and future searches for vector leptoquarks at the LHC, particularly those involving the collision of protons at high energies.

Radiation exposure during positron emission tomography (PET) scans restricts their usage for sensitive groups, such as pregnant women and young individuals requiring frequent imaging, due to compromised image quality from lower doses or shortened scan times. Deep-learning models have made significant advancements in enhancing PET images by translating low-quality PET scans with associated MRI data to higher-quality PET images, particularly with significantly reduced doses. Nonetheless, such deep learning approaches have primarily focused on utilizing training datasets similar to their test data, neglecting performance evaluation for new acquisitions outside of their distribution. We developed a novel neural network framework that incorporates the physics underlying the PET imaging process and estimates output uncertainty to address these limitations. This new uncertainty-aware neural network framework can utilize low-dose PET scans and accompanying MRI data to generate high-quality PET images at standard doses, thus enhancing robustness when processing out-of-distribution data, such as various forms of OOD PET-MRI acquisitions. Experimental results confirm the advantages of this model in enhancing PET images both quantitatively and qualitatively in various settings.

A linguistic analysis known as centering theory (CT) explains how coherence in conversations emerges from the connections between successive statements. This paper explores the link between CT and advanced computer systems that identify relationships within a text. By developing specific metrics and a search-based method, the study examines if modern computer systems that recognize connections within a text align with the principles of CT. The analysis indicates a correlation between the systems' ability to recognize connections and their ability to model the coherence of the text, but also reveals that these computer systems have limited connections to the unique characteristics of CT. Furthermore, the study shows that incorporating the concept of "centering" into the data used to train these systems significantly improves their ability to recognize connections and replicate the coherence of the text. However, the proposed systems do not capture all the aspects of CT, as indicated by the distinct patterns found through the analysis.

Recently, WiFi has become the primary method for locating individuals or devices within indoor settings. To facilitate this process, WiFi fingerprinting, a technique where reference measurements with known locations are collected and analyzed, has become a standard approach in positioning methods and algorithms discussed in academic literature. However, measuring spatial distances between these collected data sets, also known as WiFi fingerprints, relies heavily on the choice of signal distance metric employed to map signal intensity to geographical distance. To address this issue, the researchers proposed using machine learning to enhance the estimation of geospatial distances between these data sets. This research analyzed 13 diverse datasets from various open sources in order to create a universally applicable model suitable for a wide range of indoor environments. The novel approach developed extracted meaningful data features from a set of conventional signal distance metrics using feature selection and genetic algorithms. To demonstrate the versatility of this approach, models were tested on previously unused datasets from the training and validation stages. Furthermore, a comparative analysis was conducted among different machine learning algorithms utilizing a wide range of evaluation metrics, including their scalability to accommodate diverse real-world datasets.

The beam breakup instability poses a challenge for particle accelerators, particularly for energy recovery linacs with multiple beams circulating the same ring. Due to the interaction between beams, they influence one another's instability through their coupling impedance created by geometry and RF cavities. This study delves into how different filling patterns, where beams are placed in relation to each other, impact interbeam coupling and lead to varying degrees of beam destruction. By conducting simulation experiments with varying filling patterns, interbeam coupling was found to cause different amounts of beam destruction, ranging from a few percent to over ten percent in some cases. This discovery highlights filling patterns as an overlooked degree of freedom for designing multi-beam energy recovery linacs.

To extend the BFKL equation to NNLL accuracy, the one-loop CEV for two gluons with low rapidity ordering must be known. For the limit of small $p_2^+$ momentum, we derived this CEV for two gluons and found it can be expressed in terms of color generators acting on each gluon's state. When represented in the color basis, there are contributions from terms with squared Casimir $C_A$ from: gluattribution from gluattribution from gluattribution from gluattribution from gluattribution from gluattribution from quarks.

Theories explaining highly elongated polymer brush properties have provided valuable insights into the behavior of surface-grafted polymers in various scenarios. However, the parabolic model falls short in accurately describing elongated brushes on the surfaces of curved, concave substrates, like nanoparticles or certain types of block copolymer interfaces. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a zone devoid of free chain ends and demands a revised theoretical analysis. Although the 'end exclusion zone' concept has been successfully incorporated into models for cylindrical and spherical surfaces, its implications for curved surfaces with varied geometries have yet to be explored. In this study, we introduce a revised strong-stretching theory that applies to molten polymer brushes on curved surfaces of any complexity, identifying distinct regimes that give rise to end exclusion zones - including those with positive curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we predict how the size of the end exclusion zone, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching change with mean and Gaussian curvatures, offering a detailed understanding of how surface curvature affects brush geometry and free energy calculations. This comprehensive knowledge can be utilized to simulate a broad range of brush geometries encountered in the assembly of block copolymer melts.

A graph G is considered fully identifiable when a subset of its vertices R can pinpoint each vertex uniquely by determining their distance to every point in R. A sub-set of R that does this best with the fewest points is known as the minimum identifying set or "metric dimension" of the graph. Here we discuss the version of this property where the shortest distances between points are capped at some number k and call it beta_k of the graph.

Researchers explored a novel use for machine learning image processing algorithms, applying them to all-sky maps generated by the Fermi Gamma-ray Space Telescope. To simulate a year's worth of observations, they employed dictionary learning, U-net, and Noise2Noise algorithms on just one week of data. The machine learning-processed images demonstrated enhanced contrast compared to traditional methods, particularly with the u-net algorithm providing the most significant improvement. This technique successfully highlighted astronomical objects with varying brightness, including the SuperNova 1987A and the Galactic Center, while downplaying image areas with fluctuating background images. The number of models and images processed in this study was relatively small, with 25 sources of emission in a year's worth of data and a resolution of 64x64 pixels. However, machine learning application to a larger dataset with higher pixel resolution could potentially offer more accurate and up-to-date all-sky images. The study also utilized synthetic data, as actual large-scale all-sky images from instruments like the Fermi-LAT are not publicly available.

Inspired by the effectiveness of the serial dictatorship mechanism in resolving group decision-making challenges, we investigate its potential for solving a range of combinatorial optimization problems by employing a basic model where multiple agents take sequential actions. The model stipulates that each agent chooses their optimal action based on the actions taken by previous agents in the predetermined order. We aim to identify action sequences that maximize overall value for all agents involved. We establish theoretical bounds on achievable social welfare when employing a query-based approach and find that this results in a marginally improved approximation of optimal social welfare when considering a general scenario. However, when combinatorial optimization domains are in question, we demonstrate the ability to obtain high-quality approximations, achieving a $2$-approximation when applying it to specific optimization tasks including graph matching, arborescence in directed graphs, and Boolean satisfiability. We also examine issues of honesty and provide ways in which some of our solutions can be implemented fairly with incentives based on payment schemes such as the Vickrey-Clarke-Groves method. We propose and evaluate a new metric, the price of serial dictatorship, offering a quantitative indicator of the efficacy of combinatorial optimization solutions obtained via action sequences.

We designed two distinct point spread function (PSF) analysis techniques 
for detecting wide binary asteroids within wide field surveys, and subsequently
applied these to Pan-STARRS1 images featuring main belt asteroids spanning 
4 to 60 kilometers in diameter. As existing records, cited in Johnston (2019),
reveal less than 10 documented binary asteroids within this size range, with
orbital separations exceeding 10% of their primary components' Hill radius, it is 
essential to discover additional wide binary asteroids to clarify binary
stability constraints and enhance asteroid mass comprehension. Our analytical 
process for each image involved two approaches: firstly, by correlating the 
orientation of the asteroid's elliptical PSF with its sidereal motion across 
the sky, and secondly, by creating a one-dimensional profile from collapsing the 
image along the asteroid's trajectory, and comparing it to that of nearby field 
stars. Any marked deviations from typical measurements of single asteroids 
were identified and flagged; among these flagged targets, the most notable were 
designated binary prospects awaiting confirmation through high-resolution 
imaging.

This research supplements the findings related to the specified context, model, and estimation methods initially presented by Auerbach in 2019. The paper's first section explores the asymptotic behavior of the estimators presented in section 2 of the Auerbach's work. The second section investigates extensions to the model. The third section applies the model to estimate peer effects within networks. The fourth section presents results obtained from simulated data.

This study introduces novel versions of the Leibniz Rule for the Riemann-Liouville Variable-Order fractional integral and derivative. It derives key formulas, including product, quotient, and chain rules for both the integral and differential operators. Specifically, four distinct product rule formulas, four quotient rule formulas derived from product rule types, and four chain rule formulas have been established.

We introduce the G4C challenge, focusing on how natural language interactions can be guided by set objectives, which can be evaluated through the lens of a role-playing game. Specifically, we select Dungeons and Dragons as our testing ground. Within this framework, player characters represent learners with distinct identities, while the Dungeon Master functions as both a guide and authority figure tasked with leading them toward a common goal. Our methodology combines a theory-of-mind-inspired approach with reinforcement learning, training a Dungeon Master that: first learns to anticipate the players' responses to its dialogue based on past D&D conversations, then utilizes these predictions to assess the effectiveness of its guidance, which in turn propels the players toward a collective goal. Human assessments alongside automated testing reveal that a Dungeon Master trained through reinforcement learning and our baseline through theoretical mind interventions excel at achieving group objectives within a D&D setting. Moreover, our findings highlight the value of a dynamic and thoughtful NPC that considers the consequences of its language use, and the benefits of real, experienced learning communities as a source of training data for such agents.

The intricate relationship between protein knots and their folding processes is an area that biologists are actively trying to grasp. Recent research categorizes the spatial arrangements of knotted proteins using advanced topological models. A novel statistical approach, inspired by topological principles, enables the comparison of knotted protein structures based on their spatial projections. This analysis uncovers the distinctions in geometry among proteins with trefoil knots and also identifies clustering patterns according to their sequence similarities. By focusing on the intrinsic properties of these proteins in their natural state, our research uncovers various folding pathways for trefoil knots and reveals that proteins with shallow knots follow a distinct pathway compared to those with deep knots. Specifically, this study finds that proteins with shallow knots adopt a double-loop structure before folding, in contrast to proteins with deep knots that were previously found to exhibit different folding patterns. This finding is further validated through molecular dynamics simulations.

Let $\omega$ be a Kaehler form on the real $4$-dimensional torus $T^4$. Given that it fulfills an irrationality criterion which can be realized via an arbitrarily minor adjustment of $\omega$, this note proves that the smoothly trivial symplectic mapping class group of the one-point symplectic blowup of $(T^4,\omega)$ is countably infinite.

A detailed investigation of the anomalous Nambu-Goldstone (NG) theorem has been undertaken with an emphasis on its underlying mathematical structures drawn from Lie algebras, geometry, and number theory. The principles behind the anomalous NG theorem have been explored using both local Lie algebras and global Lie groups, and the phenomenon has been observed in various contexts including scalar field theory with a periodic potential, superconductivity, and color superconductivity. By examining the mathematical foundations and real-world applications, the paper provides a comprehensive understanding of the anomalous NG theorem and its far-reaching implications.

Recent studies indicate that augmenting data with counterfactual knowledge can enable models to grasp a task's causal framework, thereby producing resilient and versatile models. Nonetheless, the scale and variety of such counterfactual data are restricted when sourced from crowds and become costly to extend to new perturbation types when produced through supervised methods. To address these challenges, we present a novel framework called DISCO that generates high-quality counterfactual data at a large scale automatically. This framework prompts a general-purpose large language model to generate phrasal alterations, while a task-specific instructor model culls high-quality examples from the generated pool. We demonstrate that employing this counterfactual data in learning yields a relatively compact model that exhibits a 6% boost in robustness and 5% gain in distributional generalizability when evaluated against various rigorous metrics. Moreover, this model is 15% more adept at distinguishing genuine and counterfactual instances, as shown in evaluations conducted through both human-generated and human-AI collaborative settings.

Research into remote epitaxy on monolayer graphene holds significant promise, enabling the synthesis of highly lattice-mismatched materials and reducing waste from expensive substrate reuse. Nevertheless, concrete proof of a remote epitaxial process is yet to be found. This study discovered that prepping Heusler films through remote epitaxy actually results in a combination of remote, pinhole, and van der Waals epitaxy. When heusler films were directly deposited without using a break lock, a solely remote epitaxial process occurred. This indicated that a combination of methods must be used to achieve a remote epitaxial process. This indicated that a combination of methods must be used to achieve a remote epitaxial process. A code is referred to as $ \Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear if it results from a particular type of encoding process called the Gray image of a code that has properties derived from $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-additive code, given a prime number p greater than two. This paper specifically delves into the examination of the rank and dimension of the kernel of these $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes. Furthermore, specific limits on the rank of $\Z_3 \Z_9$-linear codes and the dimension of the kernel of $\Z_p \Z_{p^2}$-linear codes have been established and detailed examples are provided.

Conditional GANs have demonstrated superior performance in tasks requiring the generation of specific classes.  However, creating training data with multiple labels to control multiple conditions simultaneously proves impractical due to the extensive annotation required, a problem that limits the availability of such datasets in real-world applications.  This paper investigates a new setting called the single positive scenario, in which each piece of data is marked by only a single relevant label without any additional information regarding potential irrelevant labels.  A novel technique known as single-to-multi-label sampling was developed to generate multi-label data based on this single positive label annotation.  This new approach is a supplemental tool that allows current unconditional and conditional GANs to generate high-quality multi-label data while significantly reducing the required annotation. Experimental findings with real image datasets demonstrate that the technique can effectively produce accurate multi-label data even in comparison to a model trained using comprehensive multi-label data.

The GNS construction forms a correspondence between abstract collections of physical observables in a C*-algebra and associated physical states. This process essentially amounts to a reverse operation to obtain the algebra given a state. We demonstrate that the GNS construction behaves as a kind of inverse procedure for state representation through an abstract adjoint relationship, capturing fundamental aspects of the algebra's underlying properties. This abstract adjoint relationship must be seen within the context of weakly natural transformations, a concept that arises from categorifying functors. This formulation of the relationship provides the basis for interpreting the inherent mathematical structure in physical terms.

The cause behind gamma-rays in nearby galaxies emitting high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic fields reconnect, could provide a potential explanation.  By applying this "MAD" model to the 15 most radiant galaxies, we found that it can account for gamma-rays in the energy band if the matter falling into the black hole occurs at a rate that's just a tiny fraction of its potential.  However, at higher accretion rates, absorption from the abundant low-energy photons hinders the gamma-rays, thwarting the MAD model's explanation.  Moreover, using an alternate approach to describe magnetic field interactions with electrons also led to the model's failure, revealing the significance of how electrons are energized.  The model was also applied to the central black hole at our galaxy, Sgr A*, and it failed to account for gamma-rays, leading to the inference that any gamma-rays emanating from this region would be insufficient to account for high energy cosmic radiation found on Earth.

Early detection of heart conditions is crucial, and point-of-care methods like cardiac auscultation are vital for this purpose.  However, accurate abnormality detection from cardiac auscultation sounds is hampered by background noise and the variability of recording devices.  To address this challenge, this study investigates the development of effective methods to analyze cardiac auscultation sounds that have been affected by both types of distortions.  After conducting mathematical analyses of noise effects on feature extraction techniques, the authors propose using a combination of linear and logarithmic spectral features to aid a deep learning-based classifier.  The proposed method, which utilizes a Residual Neural Network (ResNet) and was tested on noisy recordings obtained from multiple stethoscopes, demonstrates a significant improvement in accuracy compared to existing approaches.  The proposed technique achieves the best results across a wide range of recording conditions and environments, indicating its potential for low-cost implementation.  The findings provide a framework for creating cardiac auscultation systems capable of accurately diagnosing conditions even in noisy environments using low-cost devices.

The proliferation of computing technology and wearable devices like smartphones and wristbands allows users to easily access health data including activity levels, sleep patterns, and sports history. Successful smart healthcare relies on training machine learning models using a large quantity of user data, but several key challenges arise. Primarily, user data exists in disparate segments, complicating data aggregation without breaching privacy protocols. Secondly, models trained on cloud platforms struggle to accommodate personalization requirements. This paper introduces FedHealth, a pioneering federated transfer learning framework for wearable healthcare designed to address these difficulties. FedHealth aggregates data via federated learning and employs transfer learning to develop personalized models. It succeeds in providing accurate, personalized healthcare without compromising security and data confidentiality. Experimentation reveals that FedHealth yields 5.3% greater accuracy in wearable activity recognition when compared to conventional approaches. Furthermore, FedHealth demonstrates versatility, extensibility, and vast potential applications in the healthcare industry.

This study classifies portfolio optimization strategies with higher order moments including skewness and kurtosis to aid Hedge Fund practitioners in navigating various paradigms and methodologies. Key research approaches, such as utility theory and multi-objective optimization, are reviewed, with an examination of their benefits and limitations.

In large-scale organizations, recruiting involves interviewing a substantial number of applicants, a time-consuming and intricate process. To achieve efficiency, a well-planned approach to selection is crucial. This process comprises multiple, interconnected problems, each mirroring a well-known computational issue. While individual research has been extensively conducted, an integrated examination of these problems is uncommon. This paper addresses two critical aspects of application processing: creating review and interview panels and scheduling interviews. We developed a prototype system to automate interview planning for a real-world scenario. Compared to existing, manual methods, our approach yields a superior plan. To demonstrate further, we evaluated two algorithmic strategies for panel creation and found they produce high-quality results. These findings can be applied to similar processes in various large-scale companies.

This study tackles a complex control issue, where the costs of transitioning between states can change suddenly in time. Our main achievement is to derive multiple ways to characterize the optimal cost function, as well as to demonstrate the existence of policies that minimize costs under this dynamic framework. Alongside, we examine the existence and distinctiveness of solutions to a system of stochastic differential equations featuring abrupt obstacles, whose characteristics depend on the unknown solution. Finally, the paper also considers the case when the underlying system includes a random movement, resulting in the optimal payoff becoming a solution to a quasi-variational HJB PDE system with discontinuous barriers. This research is an extension of prior works on smooth costs in references [8, 17].

To explore the significance of new physics, our research investigates asymmetric leptoquark pair creation in the Large Hadron Collider to provide solid constraints on its properties and aid in identifying its potential. Asymmetric production stands out from conventional methods as leptoquarks created in proton-proton collisions aren't opposite charges. To make this process possible, we outline the required conditions and list all relevant combinations of leptoquark groups that can create it. Furthermore, our studies in the Standard Model and its scalar extensions demonstrate how to integrate this process into reinterpretations of existing experiments, producing more accurate leptoquark property constraints.

We analyzed a sample of 106 galaxies for which data is available for two specific fine structure lines of neutral atomic carbon, and we found their average conditions to be significantly non-equilibrium. Based on exact solutions of a 3-level system without any assumptions regarding hydrogen gas properties, we found the line formation mechanism to be influenced by non-LTE (local thermodynamic equilibrium) excitation. This non-equilibrium state may explain recent observations of gas temperatures around 25K and is not correlated with actual gas temperatures. It also hampers our ability to determine molecular gas temperatures based on carbon isotope lines and contributes uncertainty in mass estimates for molecular gas. However, this line ratio is valuable in modeling both CO and CI spectra and is independent of radiative transfer models. It is also proposed that extreme starbursts with low line ratios and high dust temperatures could be associated with massive low-density winds and/or gas reservoirs. If verified by more detailed modeling, this may provide an additional tool for characterizing low-density gas dynamics.
